chunks: "The big advantage of a servo is feedback. Because it measures where the shaft is, it's accurate regardless of the load and it knows when it hasn't reached the target.
A stepper just counts steps and trusts that it got there, so it can lose steps without telling you. A plain DC or brushless motor doesn't know its position at all.
Second, torque holds up with speed.
A stepper's torque falls off fast as it speeds up, whereas a servo can deliver its rated torque out to its rated speed, plus short bursts of two to three times that for acceleration.
Third, efficiency. A stepper runs at full current whether or not it's doing anything, so it gets hot just sitting there.
A servo draws current in proportion to the load; at rest with no load it draws very little.
Fourth, dynamics: servos accelerate quickly, run smoothly and quietly without a stepper's step resonance, and they can reject disturbances. The downsides are cost and complexity.
You need a sensor, a driver and a tuned control loop, and a badly tuned servo can oscillate.
For light, predictable loads at low speed a stepper is simpler and cheaper, and for constant-speed jobs a plain motor with a speed controller is plenty."
